findings.title: Storage create failure recorded with the legacy duration metric
findings.body: When `d.Storage.Create` fails, the error path calls `recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)`. The failure was in unified storage, so this inflates legacy error metrics and hides storage errors. The same mix-up is in Update at line 129. It should be `recordStorageDuration`.

findings.title: Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded as storage metric
findings.body: The async legacy DeleteCollection goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)`. Legacy timings and errors are therefore attributed to storage, which corrupts both series. It should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
findings.body: The success path calls `recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, ...)`, while the error path and the legacy path use `options.Kind`. Passing the object name as a label adds a high-cardinality, inconsistent label value.

findings.title: Delete stores d.Log in context instead of the enriched logger
findings.body: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` drops the `log` with name, kind and method values that was just built. Downstream logging loses that context. It should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)`.

findings.title: Async legacy writes reuse the request context, which is cancelled when the request ends
findings.body: The goroutines derive their timeout context from the request `ctx`. That context is cancelled as soon as the HTTP request completes, so the legacy write is often cancelled mid-flight or never runs. Request-scoped values such as user identity and namespace are also still needed. The goroutines need a detached context, for example `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)`, plus the 10s timeout. The same issue is in Delete (110), Update (135) and DeleteCollection (163). The legacy copy is meant as a safety net, and this makes it unreliable.

findings.title: Legacy writes are fire-and-forget and the objects are shared with the request
findings.body: The goroutines share `obj`, `objInfo` and `options` with the request after it returns, which risks data races if these are mutated or reused. Legacy errors are only recorded in a metric and never logged. Create passes the original `obj` to legacy rather than the stored object, so server-generated fields such as the name from generateName, the UID and the resource version are missing. Legacy can then get a different identity than unified storage. Update passes the original `objInfo` to Legacy, which can compute a different result than Storage did. The old code wrapped it in `updateWrapper` to apply the stored result.

findings.title: Tests do not verify async legacy writes
findings.body: The tests never assert that Legacy Create, Update, Delete or DeleteCollection were called. Delete and DeleteCollection have no legacy mock set up, so the goroutine calls into an unconfigured testify mock and panics or races after the test finishes. The async path is also not synchronised. In the create failure case, the legacy mock is set up but should never be called, and nothing asserts that.
